title: How did we get here?
objective: Distinguish explicit rules, learning from examples, and generative output without treating them as mutually exclusive eras.
explanation: Some software follows rules people specify. Machine learning fits patterns using data. Generative AI produces content such as text or images. These approaches coexist: a generative model can be machine learning, and a product can combine models with ordinary rules. Training adjusts a model using data; inference uses the trained model. A useful test asks how a system works, not just whether its label says AI.
scenario: Three fictional tools: A sends a reminder when a timer reaches zero. B learns to label plant photos from labeled examples. C generates a new club announcement from a brief.

choices.text: A is obsolete; B and C replaced all rules.
choices.feedback: Rules still run timers, checks and many parts of AI applications.

choices.text: A uses an explicit rule; B learns from examples; C generates content and may also use machine learning.
choices.feedback: These categories overlap rather than forming a simple replacement timeline.

choices.text: All three must be conscious to work.
choices.feedback: None of these behaviors establishes consciousness.

activities.rationale: A product label is less informative than its mechanism.

activities.prompt: A trained plant model labels one new photo. What is this step?

choices.text: Training must happen again for every photo.
choices.feedback: Using a trained model does not by itself imply its parameters changed.

choices.text: Inference: applying the trained model to a new input.
choices.feedback: Right. Separate using the model from changing it during training.

choices.text: Proof that its label is correct.

activities.rationale: Inference can be wrong, especially for unfamiliar inputs.

transfer.prompt: Invent a simple rule-based tool and a tool that learns from examples. Explain how you would test the second on examples it did not train on.
rubric: Rule example has an explicit condition/action.
Learning example uses data to fit patterns.
Test includes new examples and a way to identify errors.

uncertainty: Systems can combine approaches. Do not date a single clean switch from rules to learning or infer consciousness from outputs.

optionalMedia.description: Storyboard only: three workbenches labeled rule, learned classifier, generator. Connect overlapping paths; do not portray older approaches disappearing. Provide a complete text equivalent.

branchActivity.prompt: Can a generative system also use machine learning?

choices.feedback: Generation describes output, while learning describes how patterns are fitted.

choices.text: No; they must be separate technologies.
choices.feedback: A generative model can learn from data.

branchActivity.rationale: Complete this short check, then return to the main lesson.

completionPolicy.requires: All visible required core/branch choices and required text fields

teaching.question: Is it following a rule, learning a pattern, or making something?

sections.title: Three approaches that still work together
sections.text: A rule-based tool follows a condition a person wrote: if the timer reaches zero, show a reminder. A learned classifier fits patterns from examples, such as labeled plant photos. A generator produces content, such as a new announcement. These are overlapping descriptions, not a timeline where each new approach erases the last.

sections.title: Training changes; inference uses
sections.text: During training, a model is adjusted using data. When a trained plant model labels a new photo, it is doing inference. That one prediction does not prove the label is correct or mean the model learned from the photo. A product may separately collect data for later training; do not assume it does or does not.

sections.title: Test beyond the examples it learned from
sections.text: Imagine a fictional leaf classifier trained only on clear daylight photos. A useful test includes different photos with independently checked labels, including shade or unfamiliar backgrounds. Record which predictions match and which fail. Testing only the training examples can hide a model that learned those examples but performs poorly on new ones.

practice.title: Your turn: design two tools
instructions: On paper or in your own words, invent a rule with an explicit if/then condition. You do not need to code it.
Invent a learned tool. Name the examples it would train on and the prediction it would make.
Choose two new test cases, say how you would know the expected answers, and describe a failure you would look for.
Save your designs and test plan in the final step. Use fictional objects or made-up club tasks; do not upload photos or personal data.
practice.selfCheck: Can you explain why your test examples are separate from training? What would you do if the tool fails one?

teaching.takeaway: Ask how it works, where its examples came from, and how you would check a new result.
teaching.independentPractice: Without the notes, explain a timer, a learned classifier and a generator to someone—or write the explanation yourself. Include how their functions can overlap.

references.title: Google: What is machine learning?
references.supports: Models learn patterns from data; prediction and generation. Not a claim that every software tool uses ML.
